paragraphs.text: A seed bank stores seeds so that plant varieties can be recovered if they disappear from farms or the wild. The national seed bank at Kestrel Hill, opened in 1998, now holds seeds from more than 40,000 plant species.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Before storage, seeds are cleaned and then dried in a room kept at 15 per cent humidity for about a month. Drying is essential, because seeds that contain too much water can be damaged by ice crystals when they are frozen.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The dried seeds are sealed in glass jars or foil bags and kept in underground rooms at minus 20 degrees Celsius. Under these conditions many seeds can survive for hundreds of years. Every ten years, a sample from each collection is planted to check that the seeds can still grow.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Not all seeds can be stored this way. Seeds of some tropical trees, such as cocoa, die if they are dried, so they must be kept as living plants or frozen using special techniques in liquid nitrogen.
paragraphs.label: D
